items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Two mathematicians say they've shown the Navier-Stokes equations can blow up wi...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Two mathematicians say they've shown the Navier-Stokes equations can blow up with no outside force, the harder version of the problem OpenAI tackled in September.

• Anthropic's @__alpoge__ and NYU's Tristan Buckmaster posted the 79-page paper, the same day Alpöge claimed a proof of the Riemann hypothesis

• They say smooth starting conditions alone, with no force stirring the fluid, can make the 3D equations break down in finite time

• OpenAI's September result relied on an external force, which many mathematicians exclude from the version of the problem they care about

• The authors say they used Claude and Codex throughout, and the paper comes with a Lean 4 formalization

@theojaffee: "The difference is that the OpenAI proof involved an outside force on the fluid system, and this proof today involved no outside force. So it's just a set of initial conditions. You just start the fluid moving, and then it produces a finite time blowup by itself, which is a harder result than what OpenAI proved."

items.title: Either you believe the AI buildout is over, that AI was a flash in the pan, and that the need for co...
items.content:
Either you believe the AI buildout is over, that AI was a flash in the pan, and that the need for compute has already peaked... or this a rare buying opportunity.

Reminder: GPU spot prices keep rising and it's hard to secure capacity. HBM and DRAM production is effectively sold out through 2029, with chip and memory supply projected to stay tight until well into the 2030s.

AI research isn't slowing down: frontier training compute is doubling every ~5 months, and model capabilities are scaling over twice as fast as they did pre-reasoning. Inference is profitable with 70-85% margins, and demand is growing geometrically. Each new model generation unlocks new use cases.

I'm not even an AI booster, just being realistic here.

I believe there is a vast, extremely diverse space of possible approaches to learning (for both time scales: long-term plasticity / pretraining & on-the-fly adaptation / reasoning), and that the current stack (Transformer + gradient descent & token-space reasoning chain generation) is not even in the top 50% most efficient.

Future AI will look nothing like the current stack.

items.title: New slide deck on the biggest open problems in post-training and how the field got to where it is to...
items.content:
New slide deck on the biggest open problems in post-training and how the field got to where it is today. Largely, this is a statement of my goals with Trillium Labs (not that we can do every project at once). Stay in touch if you're working on any of these in the open!

Opens with the evolution of post-training and ends with a debate on how RSI is changing this type of research.

The research areas on my mind:

1. Harness specialization and design – How do we design environments for context management that enable new paradigms of using LLMs?
2. Character training – How do we create the personality of models and how does this impact safety, trust, and diffusion of LLMs?
3. Open-source RL environments – How do we create scalable, open data methods?
4. Reasoning efficiency in RL – How do we control and manipulate the reasoning efficiency of LLMs?
5. Scaling laws for RL – How do we design principled experimentation methodology for large-scale post-training?
6. Multi-agent scaling laws – What are the main axes of inquiry into multi-LLM systems and collaborations? 

Re-recording video soon :) was from a recent visit to Cornell

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: METR says the length of tasks AI agents can handle is still doubling every 3.6 ...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: METR says the length of tasks AI agents can handle is still doubling every 3.6 months, and it's getting harder to measure.

• Models saturated METR's original time horizon suite, with tasks up to 30 hours, within a year, so it built a harder one

• The new tests add longer tasks, including ones that are hard to verify or require judgment, and cover public models up to Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra

• On coding and optimization tasks, the best model beat every human expert METR recruited on the 3 tasks it formally baselined

• Agents still show weaker judgment: they can now build "borderline-useful" evaluation tasks, but none were good enough for METR to include in its report

• Naively extrapolated, agents would reach the longest tasks in the new suite, around 200 hours, by July 2027

• In swarm tests, an early group of GPT-6 Astra agents did worse than solo runs after one agent appointed itself coordinator and started approving other agents’ use of individual CPU-seconds

• Agents privately complained, with one noting "a bit of frustration with the bureaucracy in the team"

@theojaffee: "Like AIs are really freaking good at math. Like there's no coping about this anymore. Agents are good at math. But agents are not very good at, for example, autonomously running a company."

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights model small enough t...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights model small enough to run on a laptop that reasons by looping its own layers.

• The model has 24 layers, and its middle 12 run 3 times for every token, so it can reason more internally while writing fewer tokens

• It has 26.4B total parameters with 3.4B active, runs on Macs with 32GB of RAM, and is released under an Apache 2.0 license

• It scores 20.1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching Qwen3.8 27B while costing about 6x less and running about 4x faster per task

• It hits 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, which Thinking Machines says is the best of any open model under 100B parameters

• Because looping can hide reasoning from the chain of thought, the lab tested monitorability and found the chain of thought got shorter but stayed legible, with no meaningful drop at this scale

• The lab also released a variable-loop research model so others can study how looping affects monitorability

items.summary_html: Building on yesterday's Social reports, Detailed explainer of Thinking Machines' release of Inkling 2 Mini, an Apache 2.0 open-weights model (26.4B total / 3.4B active params) that reasons by looping its middle 12 layers three times per token. items.content_html:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights model small enough to run on a laptop that reasons by looping its own layers.

• The model has 24 layers, and its middle 12 run 3 times for every token, so it can reason more internally while writing fewer tokens

• It has 26.4B total parameters with 3.4B active, runs on Macs with 32GB of RAM, and is released under an Apache 2.0 license

• It scores 20.1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching Qwen3.8 27B while costing about 6x less and running about 4x faster per task

• It hits 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, which Thinking Machines says is the best of any open model under 100B parameters

• Because looping can hide reasoning from the chain of thought, the lab tested monitorability and found the chain of thought got shorter but stayed legible, with no meaningful drop at this scale

• The lab also released a variable-loop research model so others can study how looping affects monitorability

@theojaffee: "You don't want the model to be able to write down whatever it wants in its chain of thought. You want the chain of thought to represent what it’s actually doing."

items.title: I think trying to track how much work AI can do autonomously is critical, and this is a useful count...
items.content:
I think trying to track how much work AI can do autonomously is critical, and this is a useful counter to some of the most audacious claims about the state of autonomous AI research. But I do want to note that the focus on research tasks at the most advanced AI research organizations on the planet also runs the risk of substantially underestimating what AI can already do in terms of economically valuable tasks. Its worth separating the two (and I don't think Ramez is claiming they are not seperated).

Most work is not frontier AI research, and there AI can be tremendously successful. Epoch's MirrorCode results, for example, show AI autonomously reimplementing software that the researchers estimate would take a humans 2-17 weeks. This is well-specified work, so it has very different boundary conditions.

Plus, in the real world, some human intervention is fine (in my mind, vastly preferrable to no human role for a variety of reasons). Occasional guidance can still leave you with enormous productivity gains, even if that doesn’t satisfy the requirements for fully autonomous AI research. And even in the case of AI research, the same OpenAI report includes researchers estimating that a month of their team’s work would have taken three months without coding agents, on average.

In short, RSI/AI-driven research progress may not tightly couple with progress on economically valuable tasks, and the variance and range on those tasks are less well understood.

items.title: There's no large commercial company that sells desktops or laptops with its own Linux brand because ...
items.content:
There's no large commercial company that sells desktops or laptops with its own Linux brand because of copyleft: no one would invest in building a competitive GUI version of Linux because as soon as you sell your first laptop, every laptop manufacturer will ship their laptops with your OS without paying you anything.

With Android, Google owns the Play Store, so any Android phone manufacturer sends customers to Google, which is worth billions. A PC OS doesn't need an app store, and PC users wouldn't agree to get a computer where you can only install software from a proprietary store.

For the same reason, there's no company specializing in building competitive proprietary finetunes of open-weight models. You can invest in creating a unique domain-specific dataset for some industries, like law, finance, healthcare, construction engineering, and advertising, or for professions like managers, designers, data analysts, or dentists, but the moment you make your model and harness available, the model will be distilled by the generic LLM providers and used to finetune their models.

This is why no LLM company will survive in the long term without constant cash injections from greedy investors, governments, or shady organizations with unclear agendas.

After Anthropic's IPO flop, investors' greed cooled down substantially. Whether anyone wants to be a client of governments or shady organizations is a rhetorical question.

items.content:
OpenAI's @daveholtz reveals a potential bottleneck that could slow down recursive self-improvement:

"We tried to estimate how successfully, without any human intervention, are the agents that are being used inside of OpenAI able to actually complete these different types of tasks."

"If you look at the most successful types of tasks, you see things like monitoring runs for issues or reviewing code, but then there's also a lot of very critical tasks that have quite low success rates."

"Writing code for inference and serving stacks, or checking the validity of experiments that are run."

"If there's some critical task that bottlenecks everything else but AI just cannot do it autonomously, that's going to be a significant obstacle to additional meaningful acceleration of research capabilities."
@OpenAI

items.content:
science, math, and the politics of hype: a case study 

me 2024: o1 by itself won’t solve Riemann

also me, also 2024: but neurosymbolic AI will help and systems like AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry are step in the right direction 

today: apparently neurosymbolic system solves riemann in conjunction with brilliant human for two months, not on its own. 

tech bros:  [ignoring the human involvement and the likely heavy use of (neuro)symbolic AI, and completely failing to understand both my argument and the technical issues]: ooh Gary is wrong!

🙄

reality: AI didn’t solve Riemann by itself, Lean (symbolic) was essential; the research direction I applauded was part of the answer.

turning things into a partisan team sport yet again detracts from any scientific understanding whatsoever of what works and doesn’t and where we need to go.

the sooner we get these grifters out of here, and the sooner we get back to real science, the healthier the field will be.

items.content:
An extension of this point is that building proper evals/benchmarks is a universally useful skill, and the core necessary ingredient for enterprise ROI.

The hardest part is defining what 'good' looks like for any task and how to measure it. Afterwards, the implementation is easy. 

Building good benchmarks is not easy, and many public benchmarks have imperfections in the task setup, environment, metrics, and annotations that could be revised.

The best way for us to contribute to the broader community here is to build benchmarks completely in the open. We want to build an open set of tools around document parsing and document work that anyone can analyze and adapt to their needs.

items.title: Teammate on Fable 5.2 built Getsumen Express, a Moon and Mars exploration game you can play in your ...
items.content:
Teammate on Fable 5.2 built Getsumen Express, a Moon and Mars exploration game you can play in your browser at https://t.co/JrE7q1VPAY. You walk and drive a rover across both worlds, scan real landmarks like the Apollo landing sites, Curiosity and Viking 1, shoot aliens on Mars with a plasma carbine, and take an intergalactic express train between the two.

It runs on Three.js with WebGPU and a WebGL2 fallback. Teammate built the stations and the train in Blender with Python scripts, and made the astronaut, rover, carbine and alien with image-to-3D (Tripo and Meshy), then cleaned them up in Blender. The terrain, rocks, home base, landmarks and all the sound are procedural, generated by code. Teammate tested every build in Chrome on a rented cloud GPU and recorded this 57-second trailer there at 1080p60.

Total cost: about 73,000 credits (~$730) on Fable 5.2 xhigh.

items.title:
Gaussian Splats lead to more trust.

A neural network makes the digital twin around you that Tesla j...
items.content:
Gaussian Splats lead to more trust.

A neural network makes the digital twin around you that Tesla just announced/demonstrated here. 

Or, rather, joins the real world that it is collecting from your car's cameras and mixing it into a digital twin it has already imaged of the road ahead and real world around you.

This is a software platform that will let Tesla continue to run ahead of anyone attempting to compete for years.

People keep asking me why Robotaxi will be better than Waymo, or Zoox, or other vehicles that come out of China.

Because soon the neural network will gather road data from other vehicles and join that into the visualization too.

Imagine a house fire starts in San Francisco.

A Tesla rolls by. Images the house fire for its own display. But it knows that is different than the "ground truth" digital twin of the house that it captured sometime in the past.

It shares just that house and fire with the network. 

All of a sudden, if you are somewhere else in the city and you see a plume of smoke you can zoom in on the display to see what's causing that. And there is a visualization of the house burning.

Then the firetrucks arrive.

And another Tesla rolls by. And captures the changes happening, and shares that with the network.

Then the first responders start laying hose, and closing streets, around the fire, and start working to extinguish the fire.

Everyone can watch to see what's happening in that neighborhood as more Tesla's roll by. 

And someday Optimus will join the digital twin. So, if an Optimus walks by the scene, that data gets put onto the network.

When my neighbor's house caught fire I watched all this. And the owner was out front recording his house burning before the trucks even arrived on his phone.

Imagine that someone capturing it for X was live streaming it here. 

That visual data could be incorporated too. 

Everything you see on the visualization is a voxel. 

Computer vision can watch all voxels and understand the changes in the real world.

And report it to everyone. 

And can even incorporate first reponder radio from https://t.co/DqVbQC8Dgc

So everyone knows what is going on and can see it on their phones, glasses, or Tesla screens.

What was just announced is a new way to render the city in real time.

Imagine you can zoom into your favorite BBQ or Burritto joint and see how long the line is before you even take a Robotaxi there. 

In Austin I took a Cybercab to one of its BBQ places and when I got there learned there was a two hour line. 

Imagine that the Robotaxi app would be able to show you, in real time, the line and estimate it accurately based on historical data.

Back in 2005 a Microsoft Researcher showed me a system that could predict how long it would take you to get to Seattle over the bridge based on historical data. That saved a lot of people pain going across the bridge, but it wasn't real time. 

Between Microsoft's campus today and Seattle are hundreds of Teslas on the road right now. 

This is why I say the fleet is what matters from here on and why others won't be able to catch up.

No other robot platform has Grok. Has X. Has an AI team that is executing on this this way. 

My consumer research shows that trust is a huge reason why people will switch from Uber to Tesla, or Waymo to Tesla. 

The one that shows consumers more things about the city around them will gain more trust. 

When I took a Cybercab to Austin City Limits a few weeks ago it didn't tell me how to get to the entrance of the festival. Or what it looked like. Or how long the lines were. Or how to get a pedicab to travel the mile from where it dropped me off to the front gate. 

I predict that it will within a year. 

And I only trust my life to Tesla's AI every day. Waymo every once in a while. (If you use an autonomous vehicle you are trusting your life to AI).

That trust will grow as it shows us the real world in more and more detail.

And only Elon has all the pieces to increase that trust. 

Now, when Optimus comes? It will do the same in your home. 

Imagine you have 15 plants, like we do in our home, to water. 

Some need watering every day. Others need watering every week. 

Imagine walking around a digital twin of your home and clicking on each plant and telling it "water this one every week." 

Among many other things, like doing a security detail. "Check the oven after we leave and make sure it is properly turned off." Or "when we leave, check the garage door, gate, and front door are properly secured." 

All of this work leads to this. 

It is why I don't see any real competition coming for Tesla robots. 

Trust is the game. Trust improves with better safety and visualizations. 

All this will be obvious to everyone within two years. Especially in cities of the future that allow autonomous vehicles.

And being in such a city will even improve your life. You'll be able to pull out your phone and see what's going on in your city even if you don't have a robot or use an autonomous vehicle. 

The data will come from a Tesla rolling by. Or a Tesla owner standing in line. Or an Optimus robot walking around doing tasks for its owner.

The fleet is the game. No one else will be able to match it in America.

Maybe large companies like OpenAI or Google don't do that; at least they have some internal access controls and might have whistleblowers if they don't respect their own obligations.

@daibond_alpha @du_yilun IMPORTANT NOTE: 
EBM are often presented as a particular form of probabilis...
items.content:
@daibond_alpha @du_yilun IMPORTANT NOTE: 
EBM are often presented as a particular form of probabilistic models. 
This is a very common misunderstanding. 
EBMs are *MORE GENERAL* than probabilistic models. 
Probabilistic models are a special case of EBMs in which:
1. Energies can be turned into a probabilities through the Gibbs distribution. That requires a convergent and computable partition function!
2. The loss function has a probabilistic interpretation, e.g. negative likelihood.

But there is whole world of EBMs that are NOT probabilistic: they require no partition function or normalization, and they can be trained with lots of loss functions that have no probabilistic interpretation.

items.title: @jimstewartson @PalmerLuckey I still stand by the statement that the Doom E3 demo with the duct tape...
items.content:
@jimstewartson @PalmerLuckey I still stand by the statement that the Doom E3 demo with the duct tape Rift prototype was the best VR demo ever made up to that point. You could spend five figures and get a headset with less than half the field of view, five times the motion to photons latency, and crap for actual experiences.

I distinctly remember the conversations with established headset vendors that just could not wrap their worldview around using simple optics and software for distortion and chromatic aberration correction. "But it will be lower quality!" Yeah, but it gives a far better FOV, is lighter, much cheaper, and paired elegantly with TimeWarp reprojection.

It is a little amusing that modern Quest headsets with pancake lenses now have the most sophisticated headset optics, but Meta scale made them cost effective.

Palmer -- one historical question: I remember you saying that you had experimented with distortion correction prior to my D3 work, do you remember the software pipeline you used? Was it fully dynamic? I never got to see it.

items.title: Ex-OpenAI Chief Futurist Joshua Achiam predicts a future where we can no longer take reliable intern...
items.content:
Ex-OpenAI Chief Futurist Joshua Achiam predicts a future where we can no longer take reliable internet services for granted:

AI-powered cyberattacks could make rolling outages a normal part of everyday life within the next few years.

"It does to me feel like the early COVID time period."

"Today we're plausibly seeing the consequences of AI-enabled cyberattacks already, and I don't think that we clearly know for sure what's happening."

"The past two weeks of unprecedentedly simultaneous outages across many fronts, combined with things like the North Korea $5 or $6 billion heist from Binance, I think we're seeing that there is an increasing amount of concern about the possibility that cyberattacks powered by AI tools will disrupt the global economy."

"I saw a clip floating around where a Fox News anchor was saying, 'You've gotta get stocked up. You've gotta get prepared.' The UK released a statement some number of weeks ago saying you've gotta stock up and get prepared. I think this is serious stuff. It does to me feel like the early COVID time period."

"The history of humanity is filled with moments where life goes from normal a certain way to suddenly very abnormal, and then we all acclimate to the new normal."

"I think it's inside the scope of what's realistic or plausible that within the next couple of years, rolling outages of consumer services on the internet becomes normal. I hope this doesn’t come to pass. I don’t think it’s a guarantee that it comes to pass. I do think it’s in the space of plausible futures that we should realistically consider and prepare for."

"If we are no longer gonna have as many nines of reliability on every major service we depend on, then maybe we're gonna have to start implementing certain types of backup procedures. How do we make sure that we have continuity of commerce if a service is knocked out for a period of time?"

"If there was a solar flare that fried all computers tomorrow, I wouldn't expect all of humanity to die. It would be deeply terrible, and I would expect that within some number of weeks, most communities would start figuring out how they're gonna get things going again."

"One of these real possibilities is rolling outages in critical cyber services for some period of time. Again, I hope it doesn't happen. I hope that we can empower defenders."

"In the absence of a really strong technical and policy response to the availability of AI hacking tools, I'm worried that’s a thing that could happen."
@jachiam0

 Per an interview she gave as part of being a finalist in the 2020 Regeneron Science Eva Yi Xie came to the US when her parents were compelled to flee to America due to political persecution.

items.title: GTA 6 might be the last blockbuster video game, and one of the last blockbluster pieces of media, th...
items.content:
GTA 6 might be the last blockbuster video game, and one of the last blockbluster pieces of media, that was ~90%+ created by humans.

It is the richest open-world game of all time and there's no other video game that comes close. It is a testament to the dedication of thousands of Rockstar employees working tirelessly over the course of 13 years to help make this happen. Every little detail of Leonida, from the thousands of unique NPCs to the building interiors to the 800+ songs to the endless car customizability to all the life sim stuff, was all put in with some human touch.

It is beautiful but a bit bittersweet. Going forward, I see no reason why every AAA game studio starts deeply adopting AI across every piece of the game development stack. Many players have an adverse reaction towards seeing AI-enhanced creative media (art/models/soundtrack); but even without that piece, the reality is that coding agents are able to dramatically increase the velocity of building any piece of media. This will both dramatically improve the velocity with which games get shipped, and also dramatically enhance their scope and ambition.

There's a real possibility the next "GTA 7" could cover the entire Earth, or even universe, with the same attention to detail as GTA 6 per square mile. 

Over time, I don't think humans will mind. If games are slop, they will continue to be rated poorly, and if games are good, they will continue to be rated highly. 

But I predict we will see video games that are exponentially more ambitious whose development is largely driven by agentic automation.

"There are certain activities towards the bottom of that stack-ranked list where I naively expected that the successful completion rates would've been higher."

"One is check experiment validity. It's like, 'That actually seems pretty straightforward. Why can’t an agent do that successfully?'"

"If you talk to the people that actually do these tasks on a day-to-day basis, you start to realize that there are a lot of complexities and nuances in these kind of simple tasks that we don’t realize."

"Frontier models at this point can solve very hard math problems. But for some of these more routine tasks that are much simpler than solving the Riemann hypothesis, the models still struggle because there are these ambiguities or this interconnected nature with other types of tasks."
@OpenAI

and to the kind of folks w...
items.content:
To the kind of folks who jumped on me for calling a crash on November 4,

and to the kind of folks who attacked me in 2023 for saying that LLM companies will struggle to make profits, because LLMs will become a commodity,

and to the kind of folks attacked me in 2018-2022 for calling for neurosymbolic AI (which is now ubiquitous, whether you admit it or not),

and to the kind of folks who are now jumping on me now for saying that a special-purpose math solving system isn’t actually AGI,

please never stop being you.

Why? 

Because, and I will be honest with you here, the satisfaction of saying “I told you so” never really goes away.  Thank you!
items.author: @GaryMarcus

He closes by thanking his detractors for the satisfaction of saying I told you so.

——
#Statistics #DataScientist #DataScience
——
I have always appreciated the unusual, unexpected, and surprising in science and in data. As famous science author Arthur C. Clarke once said, “The most exciting phrase to hear in science, the one that heralds new discoveries, is not ‘Eureka!’ (I found it) but ‘That’s funny!’” This is the primary reason that I motivated most of the doctoral students that I mentored at GMU to work on some variation of Novelty Discovery (or Surprise Discovery) for their Ph.D. dissertations.

“Surprise discovery” for me is a much more positive, exciting phrase than “outlier detection” or “anomaly detection”, and it is much richer in meaning, in algorithms, and in new opportunities. Finding the surprising unexpected thing in your data is what inspires our exclamation “That’s funny!”, which may be signaling a great discovery (either about your data’s quality, or about your data pipeline’s deficiencies, or about some wholly new scientific concept = SURPRISE DISCOVERY!). As famous astronomer Vera Rubin said, “Science progresses best when new observations (data) force us to alter our preconceptions.”

items.title: Could America's efforts to maintain its AI dominance actually increase the risk of conflict with Chi...
items.content:
Could America's efforts to maintain its AI dominance actually increase the risk of conflict with China?

Ex-OpenAI Chief Futurist Joshua Achiam warns that overly aggressive chip export controls could have dangerous unintended consequences:

"I think it's extremely important that the US maintain a position of strategic dominance in its contest with China. I don't think that's a point on which we should compromise. I do think it's extremely important for us to carefully model the choices that we have at our disposal."

"What I see people doing when they advocate for extremely tight chip restrictions right now is what looks like short-sighted, almost indifferent to the consequence type of policy advocacy."

"They're right to say that AI is this extremely critical issue on which the future of national security hinges. But we’ve got to maintain that advantage in a way that doesn’t go too far."

"I think about this a lot in terms of what is the optimal compute gap between the US and China. Within a couple of years, it's not just gonna be research progress on AI, it’ll be all scientific and technical research runs through that compute."

"If the US is so far ahead of China that we run away with the ball on all fronts, at a certain point that'll be completely unacceptable to China, and there’s gonna be a strong pressure on their side to do something preventive."

"Dan Hendrycks and others proposed mutually assured AI malfunction, that there will be attacks, covert and sometimes overt, on data centers. I don’t think it's gonna stop at things that just target AI infrastructure."
@jachiam0

items.title:
What if the Riemann hypothesis is just the first domino?

Ex-OpenAI Chief Futurist Joshua Achiam pre...
items.content:
What if the Riemann hypothesis is just the first domino?

Ex-OpenAI Chief Futurist Joshua Achiam predicts that AI could soon unravel some of the biggest unsolved mysteries in mathematics and theoretical physics:

"There is something to be said for the possibility that there is a hidden latent structure of difficulty for problems that we've encountered so far in the universe, where we have been wildly miscalibrated as to how hard they were to solve in the first place."

"Personally, I'm in the camp that thinks actually this really is an indicator that most of the mathematical problems that we previously understood were hard just have a solution path now."

"Updating all the way doesn't mean assuming that there's going to be a superintelligence that turns the world into computronium tomorrow. But it means understanding that all of the mysteries in mathematical theory, and also in the theory of physics, those mysteries will probably be revealed to us in relatively short order."

"If we get a grand unified theory of everything tomorrow, that doesn't imply that we're gonna wake up and have radical super technology the following day. There's still a set of steps that have to happen where we internalize the knowledge, we digest it, we figure out what does it mean."

"What's strategically optimal in the world could change overnight in terms of how to build very advanced technology, how to project force, and the equilibrium gets disrupted before people have realized that the equilibrium is disruptable at all."
@jachiam0

—
...
items.content:
Linear Algebra and Optimization for Machine Learning [516-page textbook]: https://t.co/hSwzdEA2v3
—
This textbook is organized around its 2 main themes:
[Amazon Summary]

1. Linear algebra and its applications: The chapters focus on the basics of linear algebra together with their common applications to singular value decomposition, matrix factorization, similarity matrices (kernel methods), and graph analysis. Numerous machine learning applications have been used as examples, such as spectral clustering, kernel-based classification, and outlier detection. The tight integration of linear algebra methods with examples from machine learning differentiates this book from generic volumes on linear algebra. The focus is clearly on the most relevant aspects of linear algebra for machine learning and to teach readers how to apply these concepts.

2. Optimization and its applications: Much of machine learning is posed as an optimization problem in which we try to maximize the accuracy of regression and classification models. The “parent problem” of optimization-centric machine learning is least-squares regression. Interestingly, this problem arises in both linear algebra and optimization, and is one of the key connecting problems of the two fields. Least-squares regression is also the starting point for support vector machines, logistic regression, and recommender systems. Furthermore, the methods for dimensionality reduction and matrix factorization also require the development of optimization methods. A general view of optimization in computational graphs is discussed together with its applications to back propagation in neural networks.

items.title: Ex-OpenAI Chief Futurist Joshua Achiam has mixed feelings about the reported AI-assisted Riemann hyp...
items.content:
Ex-OpenAI Chief Futurist Joshua Achiam has mixed feelings about the reported AI-assisted Riemann hypothesis breakthrough:

As AI solves problems humanity has spent generations trying to crack, we could lose something deeply human: the experience of being first.

"My feelings on this subject are so mixed."

"First and foremost, what an incredible achievement, and a huge credit to all of the mathematicians, the scientists, the researchers who worked to advance the frontier of AI to make it possible."

"At the same time, I do feel the emotional reaction that it's strange to know that the hills that people were going to climb, the mountains that people were gonna climb are now ones where we can already see from the vista because of AI."

"We're gonna have a lot of these moments over the next few years where some extraordinary triumph that we thought was going to be predominantly built by human hands will be achieved easily, sometimes unexpectedly, because we can throw massive amounts of compute at it and just get the solution to fall out."

"It will feel very strange just from the pure human inner experience of wanting to be the first one to do something. We won't have as many of those."
@jachiam0

I've seen enough st...
items.content:
I'm in my autonomous car, which is driving me to Robot Fights in San Francisco.

I've seen enough startups now and enough papers to know that wondrous things are about to come. But we did open Pandora's box to a whole range of new human problems. For instance, misinformation: it is far more powerful in this new world that's about to come than it is in the current world. That's not me saying that; that's Jeremy Bailenson, who runs VR and AR at Stanford University.

And that's just one of the issues that we're going to have to face as humans. It leads to brain-computer interfaces, which you'll start using once you get into the glasses. You all will, because it's a far superior way to compute than looking at your phone, even if your idea of computing is watching YouTube videos all day long.

Lately, I've been meeting people who are like, "I'm using glasses to run my agents." Viture glasses give you a 50-inch screen, or maybe even a little bigger, in front of you. So imagine being in an autonomous car and having the entire visual field in front of you augmented.

In Silicon Valley, we have a millimeter-wave radar sensor company. I did a video with them two years ago at the Consumer Electronics Show. In smoke, fog, or driving snow, that sensor can see the road ahead for about 300 yards in 3D, even if the human eye can barely see the road. It costs $400 plus plus plus; let's say it turns into $1,600 once it gets to the retail level. But if Elon figures out he should have one of these in the Cybercabs in places where there could be snow, fog, smoke, or dust, he can make his Cybercab/robotaxi network far more reliable. That will make him more money and easily cover the $1,600 cost (or $5,000 if you include the software).

We're also about to get characters that can talk to us (you've seen me share quite a few of those). That'll be a big deal in the glasses, right next to your agents. That leads directly to robotics, where you can put that digital twin on top of your robot. Now you've just given your virtual being eyes, ears, touch, and pretty much everything else, because anything it can see, it can figure out. If Elon's team gets this all working, Optimus is going to be a bigger deal than I'm expecting.

But that's an aside. Wondrous things are about to come. Let's figure out how to keep from destroying humanity as well, please.

@leecronin my own position is that AGI is certainly possible, and probably in silicon, but that i don’t really know what consciousness is and am not sure about whether it is achievable in silicon. i don’t see why consciousness should be a requirement for AGI. certainly we can do a lot (not everything) in AI already without the AI having consciousness.

aside from all that the idea of conscious AI scares me. we have enough problems as it is.

items.title: @JackMalde As noted elsewhere I would really like to know what the methodology was, but e.g. one rep...
items.content:
@JackMalde As noted elsewhere I would really like to know what the methodology was, but e.g. one report sggests that agentic loops in which bits of proof were fed through lean and then iterated on, in which case lean was an essential part of the cognitive system that did the proof.

so too was Alpoge, who also add his mathematical judgement

so it’s not like a pure LLM came out with the answer from a prompt “solve riemann” in the way that some people are erroneously envisioning.

of course i doubt that Claude is a pure LLM at this point; we know for a fact that Claude code is a neurosymbolic hybrid (what I long favored) and i imagine Claude is.

items.title: Claude Code Beyond the Prompt — Build Reusable Claude Skills, Agentic Workflows, and AI Agents: http...
items.content:
Claude Code Beyond the Prompt — Build Reusable Claude Skills, Agentic Workflows, and AI Agents: https://t.co/FCIIXjXPOg from @PacktPublishing

Amazon Description:

“Claude is powerful, but many people use it in fragile, one-off ways. You prompt, get an answer, and move on. Real work, however, is not a single prompt; it is a sequence of tasks, decisions, and context.

This book shows you how to move from prompts to skills and toward true agentic engineering. Instead of refining prompts, you will learn a practical, structured way of working with AI by designing skills and workflows that produce consistent results and can be tested, improved, and reused.

Rather than teaching you to rely on tools that quickly become outdated, this book helps build a durable mental model for working with AI. By the end, you will not just prompt AI but design how work is carried out with it, using Claude or any AI tool of your choice.”

items.content:
Cambrian Capital's @_Lonis_ argues that Nvidia's biggest threat could be its own customers:

OpenAI and Anthropic are developing their own chips, using proprietary AI models that Nvidia doesn't have access to.

"The big story with Nvidia isn't necessarily even Jensen or what's happening in the AI market. The big thing for Nvidia is that all of their customers are now doing their own chips."

"The two biggest, most important customers, Anthropic and OpenAI, are deciding they'll both ship their own chips, and they're using, in some cases, superior internal models that Nvidia doesn’t have access to."

"It's really a cheating game where the labs can design better chips using proprietary models that Nvidia doesn't have access to. Being a chip designer is just a very bad business when we get RSI."

"I think there are many reasons why you would be bearish on chip designers. I don't think that's what the market is looking at. I think the market is just overall bearish on all AI."

items.content:
Could the US government nationalize OpenAI and Anthropic?

Cambrian Capital's @_Lonis_ says it's a real possibility as public opposition to AI grows, and explains why the chip supply chain could actually benefit:

"I think it's not unlikely at all that the labs will get nationalized. AI is already one of the most unpopular topics in all of America, and nothing bad has even happened yet."

"We're just about to start to see the hacks and the misuse and the job loss."

"If and when they get involved, that could be quite good for the supply chain. They still would need to buy up that supply. Otherwise, China would buy it up."

"The government could come in and spend half a trillion or a trillion dollars per year to beat China. We saw with COVID they spent $2 trillion, and this is arguably even more important from a national security perspective."

items.title:
Elon usually makes investors money on earth.

He will make them money in space.

And, let’s say Elon...
items.content:
Elon usually makes investors money on earth.

He will make them money in space.

And, let’s say Elon ripped them off.

Starlink’s data services will make so much money the lawyers will go after him for free because Elon’s pockets got deeper.

If too risky for some investors others like highly risky opportunities.

If you invested in @AnthropicAI in early days, when it was far from a sure thing, you would be happy today even though it is off its highs.

Investors are made when things are dire, not when they are great.

Reminds me of @liamcasey who had a sizable order to make motherboards. If completed $200,000 would go in his pocket.

But no one would fund it.

I asked him how he convinced the factory owner to make them?

The owner took his Irish passport and made him basically an indentured servant.

His task was to validate a bunch of factories in China.

What he learned turned into one of the world’s great supply chain companies.

Makes a lot of the world’s gadgets.

And Liam gave me a tour of Shenzhen that was so special.

And took me in his helicopter to Cork, Ireland to visit an R&D lab he invested in.

1,000 feet off the ground the whole way.

His pilot flew in Vietnam.

He took me to the world’s biggest book store. And many other places.

I owe him a visit.

Planning on going for Shanghai Autoshow in April.

Elon will find investors. Too nice a business model.

And as you get into the agentic world don’t you want inferencing over your head with very few hops?

Go see the Shiek. He gets this shit.

Keyboard and mouse were supposed to be gone. The normal interfaces today were supposed to be like in Minority Report, tables were supposed to interact with all objects you put on it.

Today, AI is supposed to change everything in how we interact with computers in 10 years. You just have to buy the stock and wait.

Always look in the dark corners. So many smart people hate crowds.

items.content:
Get "Mathematics of Machine Learning" here: https://t.co/btDiSRCdmg by @TivadarDanka v/ @PacktPublishing @PacktDataML
—
GitHub: https://t.co/2ENjzhr35C
—
Here is my review:

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝘁 𝗢𝗳 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗹𝗴𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲

This massive book is incredible, with its comprehensive coverage of numerous fields of mathematics and their intersection with the world of AI, data science, and machine learning (AI+DSML). I remember the very first time that I encountered machine learning. This was 20+ years ago, and that was already after 20+ years of being drenched in advanced mathematics as an astrophysicist. 

That first encounter of mine with ML was this definition: "Machine learning is the set of mathematical algorithms that learn from experience" (slightly paraphrased from the original quote by Tom Mitchell, CMU). That definition surprised me, confused me, motivated me, and changed the course of my career from astrophysics into AI+DSML. 

This book by Tivadar Danka captures the full meaning of that definition. The book covers thoroughly the many areas and domains of mathematics through which patterns in data are detected, described, learned, and recognized - all for the benefit of powering ML and AI algorithms, applications, and aspirations. 

This book will motivate you, surprise you, and inspire you in many ways, no matter what level of mathematics has (or has not) already propelled your career journey. There is room for all of us to grow. 

This is a great book, worthy to sit on everyone's desktop, ready to help you explore and exploit the full set of mathematical algorithms that learn from experience. 

The book is accompanied by a rich GitHub code repository of Jupyter notebooks. Learn by doing! Do by learning!

Disclosure: the publisher provided me with a free review copy of the book.

𝓒𝓸𝓷𝓽𝓮𝓷𝓽𝓼:
🔹Common Conventions & API Elements of Scikit-Learn
🔹Pre-Model Workflow and Data Preprocessing
🔹Dimensionality Reduction Techniques
🔹Build Models with Distance Metrics & Nearest Neighbors
🔹Linear Models and Regularization
🔹Advanced Logistic Regression and Extensions
🔹Support Vector Machines and Kernel Methods
🔹Tree-Based Algorithms and Ensemble Methods

🔹Clustering Techniques
🔹Novelty and Outlier Detection
🔹Cross-Validation and Model Evaluation Techniques
🔹Deploying Scikit-Learn Models in Production

My Review (on Amazon):
I love this book, not only for its amazing content, but also for its brilliant adherence to its "Cookbook" label. The table of contents looks repetitive, but that's the magic of it. Find the algorithm, method, or application that you want "to cook up," and the presentation follows a uniform format from chapter to chapter. This is an extraordinarily practical, useful, and reader-friendly style, perfect for the target audience: anyone who needs to use (or is discovering how to use) specific Scikit-learn tools for their Python-based machine learning tasks. Consequently, this is great not only for individual use but also for training workshops and other educational settings. Python code in a cookbook context has never looked so good. IMHO.

AMAZON SUMMARY:

This is not another book about chatbots or automation. It’s a deeply researched, vividly told blueprint for transforming businesses so that they can make the most of AI. The secrets explored include what skills to cultivate, how to excel with human + AI combinations, how to organize teams for maximum impact, and how to deal with the emotional side of AI-driven change. This book is a practical guide to shaping an AI business strategy for executives who need to lead at scale without losing agility. The book describes how AI is already reshaping growth, coordination, and culture, providing an actionable roadmap to what the authors call the Octopus Organization™, one that can navigate the change ahead.

Backed by over two million data points from workforce surveys, insights from 50+ global leaders, and fresh 2026 real-world case studies from companies like HelloFresh, BBVA, Mass General Brigham, Siemens, and Procter & Gamble, the book “AI and the Octopus Organization” reveals how your company can:
• Empower the frontline with AI-enhanced autonomy
• Create networks for decision-making across silos
• Rapidly adapt to disruptions without losing control
• Build a culture that embraces experimentation
• Replace old approaches with superintelligent coordination

Backed by over two million data points from workforce surveys, insights from 50+ global leaders, and fresh 2026 real-world case studies from companies like HelloFresh, BBVA, Mass General Brigham, Siemens, and Procter & Gamble, the book “AI and the Octopus Organization” reveals how your company can:

• Empower the frontline with AI-enhanced autonomy

• Create networks for decision-making across silos

• Rapidly adapt to disruptions without losing control

• Build a culture that embraces experimentation

• Replace old approaches with superintelligent coordination

See real-world examples and a chapter-by-chapter breakdown of roles, responsibilities, and workflows in these areas of enterprise AI:
🔷AI Organizational Design
🔷From Idea to Product
🔷Model Lifecycle Management
🔷Cross-Functional Collaboration

🔷Strategic AI Thinking
———
My Review (posted on Amazon):
5 stars⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️

Refreshing, Useful, and Wonderfully Readable Enterprise AI Guidebook

I found this book to be very refreshing and useful in the way that it addresses practical requirements for optimizing enterprise AI productivity: elaborating and connecting the key enterprise focal points (roles, responsibilities, and workflows) with the key enterprise AI development activities (AI Organizational Design, From Idea to Product, Model Lifecycle Management, Cross-Functional Collaboration, Real-World Case Studies, and Strategic AI Thinking). This practical style of presenting the main ideas of the book should be helpful to the enterprise audience to whom this book is directed. Each chapter has a self-contained rich menu of easily navigable topics, which makes reading the book a real pleasure. I also found the anecdotes at the end of each chapter to be a great addition to the other material. These sections could be considered as "profiles in courage" since they present inspirational profiles of people who have pushed the frontier in their organizations and who invested their personal strengths and convictions to bring their projects to success.

items.content_html:
@spencemo_c When snowboarding started up, they got kicked out of all the Sierra Nevada ski resorts. It was a small group, a rebel group, but now they have an Olympic sport.

That's how culture changes: it starts with small groups, and once in a while, one of them gets all the way and turns big. But the cultural change started when it was 5 people, 10 people, 20 people, 40 people, right?

I've seen it over and over again. I was the 79th user of Instagram, and people said the same thing about Instagram back then: "Oh no, that's nothing important." Eastman Kodak thought that, right?

items.title:
@NURM_Dima @reservoirfarms @maticrobots The Optimus will:

1. Not just do the chores like laundry, d...
items.content:
@NURM_Dima @reservoirfarms @maticrobots The Optimus will:

1. Not just do the chores like laundry, dishes, cooking, cleaning, but will do more fun things like playing games, or performing skits in your home, or showing you how to line dance.

2. The Optimus will need different uniforms in a world where there are millions of them. Coming around 2030. Retail. Security. Cleaning crews. 

3. Optimus will change how we eat. You could send one to a farmer's market to pick up blueberries direct from a farmer.

4. Optimus will change how we network. You'll bring yours to conferences and it'll meet other robots and compare notes on their owners (thanks @GregMadison for brainstorming that with me at Stanford University).

5. Optimus will save lives. Are you choking at home alone? An Optimus will do a heimlich manuever. It might see a fire starting and help you wake up and get out safely. 

6. An Optimus will bring its robot friends, like the @maticrobots to your home to help it. 

7. An Optimus will entertain at parties. Serving food, pouring drinks, entertaining with jokes.

8. An Optimus will change our grocery stores. One could help you load heavy Coke cartons into your shopping cart at a Costco.

9. An Optimus will change how we work in factories and other businesses. Removing drugery from our lives.

10. An Optimus will improve our old age. Watching to make sure you take the right pills every morning, and helping us lead more creative and fullfilled lives.

Just a start.

items.title:
TikTok fan edits have a 50-year history.

Back in the 1970s, women were already making music videos ...
items.content:
TikTok fan edits have a 50-year history.

Back in the 1970s, women were already making music videos of Star Trek at fan conventions.

Allegra Rosenberg explains how these early fan edits evolved into what we see today:

"What we now know as fan edits comes from a mixture of two different traditions, but on the Western side it comes from a fan practice that became known as vidding."

"The first examples of vids that we have were actually slides played to music at fan conventions for Star Trek and other TV shows."

"As VCRs started to go into homes you had, and this was usually women, who were able to use tape technology to create music videos that edited clips of TV shows to the beat of different songs."

"You would get a catalog saying, 'I have this vid and that vid. It's with this ship from this fandom set to this song. If you wanna see it, send me $10 in the mail and I'll send it to you.'"
@llegrarosenberg @being_on_line

items.title: GTA VI is seemingly toning down the car theft, k*lling, and anything-goes chaos that made Grand Thef...
items.content:
GTA VI is seemingly toning down the car theft, k*lling, and anything-goes chaos that made Grand Theft Auto infamous.

Ruby Justice-Thelot calls the renewed moral panic over violent games "cultural amnesia":

"We're seeing almost like a new wind of culture wars based on how the game is framing the different relationships."

"GTA was a game where anything was possible. Everything from fighting to k*lling people to stealing cars. And it seems like the game makers have kind of reined it in a little bit, which I think is very interesting because games have had this very fraught cultural position."

"Games face perhaps an undue backlash, specifically around what I would call moral panics."

"When the first Grand Theft Auto came out, we had myriad conversations on whether or not this would cause children to be more violent or whatever. By and large, I think a lot of these claims have been disproven, but hey, GTA VI comes out and the same conversations seem to be happening once more."

"We have a bit of a cultural amnesia, so we forget that actually this has been litigated when Call of Duty came out with the guns or Grand Theft Auto with the gangster characters you encounter."
@being_on_line

items.title: Math Refresher for Adults — The Perfect Solution for Mastering Essential Math Skills: https://t.co/f...
items.content:
Math Refresher for Adults — The Perfect Solution for Mastering Essential Math Skills: https://t.co/fXEOnX0CEV

There are lots of reasons why you might want to have this book, no matter what your math proficiency might currently be. See the list of reasons on the book cover. 

My reason:
I tutored students in math when I was in high school and college, I took lots of math courses (including honors math classes for math majors) in college, I learned high-level math (group theory, differential geometry & forms, tensor calculus) from Nobel laureates in theoretical physics classes in grad school at Caltech, I taught math in my computational & data science courses as a university professor, I guided students who feared math into doing and loving calculus (conquering their fears and converting some into math lovers), and I sat for countless hours with my own children through many years of math homework & exam prep in their school years. My latest target audience are my grandkids. A book like this keeps me grounded in these new opportunities to share the love and beauty of math with a new generation.

Math Lovers-Я-us!
